newsitem.title: USA: Liposome stock plunges on test drug failure.
newsitem.headline: Liposome stock plunges on test drug failure.

text.p: Liposome Co. Inc., which had been one of the most popular investments in the biotech sector, lost more than 61 percent of its value Wednesday after the company said a promising new drug failed clinical trials.
The news, issued before the market had opened, was a blow to the small drug maker and to many Wall Street analysts who had been recommending Liposome to investors.

Liposome's stock plunged $15.25 to $9.56, wiping out about $570 million in market capitalisation. The company was the biggest loser of the day and the most active issue on Nasdaq, with more than 29 million shares changing hands.

Princeton, N.J.-based Liposome said patients taking its Ventus drug for acute respiratory distress syndrome, or ARDS, responded no differently in a Phase III clinical trial than those who were given a placebo.

"We are very disappointed in the results of this study," Chairman Charles Baker said in a statement. "We will continue to evaluate the drug to determine whether it can play a role in the treatment of patients with ARDS. We will also continue to evaluate whether it may be useful in other clinical settings."
Investors had expected Ventus to show clear efficacy and become a standard treatment for ARDS, a currently untreatable condition that afflicts hundreds of millions of Americans.

In an interview on CNBC cable television, Baker said the drug had the potential to generate revenues of $1 billion a year. Liposome currently has just one drug on the market, Abelcet for systemic fungal infections. Abelcet generated $16 million in revenues in the latest quarter.
Other Phase III trials of Ventus are ongoing.

With an earlier Phase II trial of Ventus appearing to show it worked, expectations ran high that the Food and Drug Administration would approve it by next year, making Liposome one of the biggest success stories in biotech and a favourite among Wall Street analysts.
"Its list of recommendations read like a "Who's Who on Wall Street," said Evan Sturza, an analyst with Sturza's Institutional Research.

Hambrecht & Quist, which had served as the company's underwriter, downgraded the company to a hold from a buy Wednesday, noting the lack of the key drug removed the "explosive upside potential" for the company's stock.

Sturza and some other analysts who had not recommended the stock questioned whether the company had raced through the approval process without giving enough consideration to the complex issues involved in the treatment of ARDS.
A severe respiratory disorder that often afflicts people who are already close to death, ARDS causes inflammation in the lungs and sometimes results in patients suffocating from a fluid buildup.

Because patients with ARDS usually suffer from other ailments, as well as from the debilitating effects of prolonged used of a ventilator, it can be hard to determine whether a drug designed specifically for the respiratory illness is working. Many patients may show some improvement in lung capacity but die anyway from other complications.

But some analysts offered a more troublesome reason for Lipsome's longstanding popularity on Wall Street. They said the company's aggressive courtship of investors through frequent equity offerings generated a lot of business for underwriters and appeared to create a positive bias.

"It's a bit of a mystery to me which is the chicken and which is the egg, but typically companies that do a lot of offerings tend to have better sponsorship," said Jim McCamant, editor of the Medical Technology Stock Letter, which follows several biotech companies.

Marc Ostro, one of the analysts had recommended the company, resigned from UBS Securities on Wednesday after the bad news came out. Ostro had had a particularly close relationship with Liposome, having served as president of the company in the 1980s. UBS declined to comment on the reason for his departure.
